summary: Pig Point light at the mouth of the Nansemond River, Virginia: lit 1878 on a sixth-order lens, dismantled 1935, discontinued 1974.

structures.note: Hexagonal wooden cottage with the light on top. Torn down 1935 (USLHS). Foundation described as screw pile (USLHS, Suffolk River Heritage) or cast-iron-sleeved wood piles (Board 1879 as quoted by LighthouseFriends; Chesapeake Chapter).

access.note: No light stands at the site today (LighthouseFriends). The station was not open to the public (USLHS). Site on the water off Pig Point.

Deactivated and dismantled 12 December (Chesapeake Chapter timeline). USLHS dates the discontinuance to 1935.

corrections.why: USLHS disposition: the superstructure was torn down in 1935 and a steel skeletal tower was placed on the old foundation. The wooden tower no longer stands. Record's 'standing' comes from the uslhs structure entry, which predates the disposition.

The Board's 1879 report as quoted by LighthouseFriends calls the structure a sleeve-pile structure, and the Chesapeake Chapter says screwpiles were judged too hard for the river bottom. USLHS and Suffolk River Heritage say screw pile. For editor review; the sources disagree.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: USLHS gives Portsmouth, VA as the town. The Chesapeake Chapter places the light at Pig Point in Suffolk. Both put it on the east side of the river entrance. The story names neither city.

The record's 1935 follows USLHS and LighthouseFriends. The Chesapeake Chapter timeline says the old light was deactivated and dismantled on 12 December 1934, with the automated light in service by 25 February 1935. The two dates can both be right if 1935 is the year the new light was established, but the sources do not say so.

Temple Ripley: USLHS and LighthouseFriends end his service in 1933, the year of automation. Suffolk River Heritage ends it in 1924. The Chesapeake Chapter says at least 1926. The story gives the roster's 1908 to 1933.

notes_for_editor: Moderate evidence, mostly secondary. Primary Light-House Board text for 1876-1879 and 1933-1935 was not in the local corpus (the corpus holds 1891-1901 Board volumes), so the construction story rests on LighthouseFriends' quotations and the Chesapeake Chapter timeline. The 1899 lens question is open: the Board's report says 'new model fifth-order lamps were supplied'; the Chesapeake Chapter says the lens was replaced. Keeper disagreements to resolve: Rufus E. Potter (roster 1878-1881, Suffolk 1878-1885); P.S. Midgett (roster first assistant 1922-1933, Chesapeake Chapter head keeper at least 1930); Ripley's end date. The 1935 Darden account is from Suffolk River Heritage only; the sources do not agree on its date relative to the December 1934 deactivation. The stated fog-bell detail and the 1933 $3,420 saving come from the Chesapeake Chapter only. The record's coordinates (OpenStreetMap 36.91481, -76.445149) sit about 70 m from LighthouseFriends' position (36.914722, -76.444444); not a correction. The record's OpenStreetMap 'conflict' (a structure mapped today) is unexplained in the sources read: LighthouseFriends says no light exists at the site, and the story says so without claiming what remains. No wreck, storm or rescue tied to this light was found in the sources read; the Life-Saving Service wreck tables name the river only as a port. Lens: the sixth-order lens from 1878; fifth-order from 1899 per the Chesapeake Chapter. Fact-check 2026-10-28: all 102 quotes were found on the first run. The 51 roster lines match roster.py exactly, with person slugs. Checked against the USLHS record, LighthouseFriends ID=1932, the Chesapeake timeline and article, the Suffolk River Heritage page, the fiscal-1899 Board report (scan 140) and the Evening Star of 27 August 1915 (page 18). The Evening Star OCR reads 'John Marehant'; the story's 'John Marchant' matches USLHS (John M. Marchant, 1913-1916). The roster's 40 first-assistant lines are entries, not people (Ella L. Edwards and Edward L. Thomas each appear twice). Suffolk River Heritage's keeper list gives 'Mrs. Ella L. Edwards' as keeper for 1903-1906 and Ripley to 1924; the story says the roster's first-assistant dates only and gives the 1924 and 1926 disagreements. The Chesapeake article gives 1935 for the deactivation, the timeline 1934 (12 December); both are now stated. The metalwork: LighthouseFriends, quoting the Board, says part of it came from the Roanoke Marshes foundation; the timeline does not say how much. Fixed in the text: the white-cottage and shoal citations, the metalwork overstatement, the 'forty first assistants' count, the disputed Ripley end dates, the 1935 deactivation, the letter's second-hand schooner count, and the Commissioner's title.
